Topology began with a puzzle about a city.

The paper's title calls the subject *geometria situs*, the geometry of position.
That is exactly the move a smooth layer makes: it may stretch the plane, but it cannot change which region surrounds which.

Noether's 1925 observation turned Betti numbers into homology groups, and that shift is what makes the shape of data computable (\cite[McLarty, 2006]{mclarty2006noether}).

Once holes are group elements, they can be tracked across a growing radius: Edelsbrunner, Letscher and Zomorodian's persistence algorithm records when each hole is born and when it dies (\cite[Edelsbrunner et al., 2002]{edelsbrunner2002persistent}), and Zomorodian and Carlsson gave the efficient algebraic formulation (\cite[Zomorodian & Carlsson, 2005]{zomorodian2005}).
The output is a barcode — a summary of which loops are robust structure and which are noise.
[Geometry III](geometry_iii) develops the algebra; here it is the bridge from "the data is knotted" to a measurable claim.
The egg is a *surrounding*; a nastier tangle is a *link* — two rings threaded through each other like a chain, which you cannot pull apart without cutting.

Colah's point is that a network classifying such data is, in the language of knot theory, performing an **ambient isotopy**: a *continuous family of homeomorphisms* that deforms one configuration into the separated one, the data moving smoothly and never tearing.
The continuous layer-by-layer visualization is not just a pretty animation — it is the isotopy itself, made visible.
There is a trap worth naming, because it is the trap an optimizer actually falls into.
Faced with an entangled pair of manifolds, the *genuinely* correct move is to pull them cleanly apart into a new dimension.
The *lazy* move is to leave the tangle in place and just **stretch the thin bits until they are near-singular** — pulling the boundary into an ever-thinner sliver that threads the gaps.
This can reach high training accuracy, so it presents itself as a tempting local minimum, with very high derivatives and sharp near-discontinuities exactly where the stretching happens.
The tell is in the decision grid: instead of two clean regions, you get a boundary that snakes and thins to a hair.
The standard countermeasure is a **contractive penalty** — regularize the derivative of each layer so the network is charged for precisely this kind of near-singular stretching.
It pushes training back toward the honest isotopy.
(In the egg demo, a width-2 net that "almost" works by snaking a boundary is doing exactly this.)

The final readout is a flat cut.

So "folding" and "topology" are not two ideas; they are the *same* idea read from two directions.
A network must move data through space to make a flat cut work.
If the moves are homeomorphisms, topology dictates exactly how many extra dimensions the journey requires.
If the moves are allowed to fold, the network spends those same dimensions as creases.
The manifold hypothesis is an empirical claim, not a definition: natural data — images, sounds, word vectors — concentrates near a low-dimensional manifold inside its high-dimensional ambient space.
Fefferman, Mitter and Narayanan give statistical tests for estimating a manifold's dimension and reach from finite samples (\cite[Fefferman et al., 2016]{fefferman2016testing}).
That matters here because the width argument is only as good as the premise: if the data were truly high-dimensional, there would be no low-dimensional tangle to separate.

This is the **manifold hypothesis** made mechanical \cite{fefferman2016testing}: natural data sits on low-dimensional manifolds, and classification is the business of **separating tangled manifolds**.
The theorem you can take away is a clean one —
> For smooth, strictly monotone layers, a network's reach is bounded by its **width**: > depth can move the data, but it cannot change its topology.
To un-knot the data, the > network must be allowed to think in *more dimensions than the data itself has*.
The topology program has produced results about networks, not only metaphors.

Olah's original argument is the smooth-layer case: with full width and a strictly monotone activation, every layer is a homeomorphism onto its image, so a width-two stack can never separate a disk from a surrounding ring (\cite[Olah, 2014]{colah2014manifolds}).
The barrier is not about depth: adding layers cannot buy a dimension.
What buys it is width, or a non-injective activation such as ReLU, whose folds are the subject of the [Origami chapter](origami) (\cite[Keup & Helias, 2022]{keup2022origami}).
Neural persistence carries the same tools into trained networks (\cite[Rieck et al., 2019]{riek2019neural}).
That is the geometry of thought: not a set of numbers to memorize, but a shape to be untangled, one reversible stretch (or one well-placed fold) at a time.
